review.debrief: Successful treatment can create a new monitoring problem. Recovery should be judged across filtration, perfusion, balance and electrolytes rather than one improving marker.
review.conflict: Creatinine improves while high urine output, thirst, falling weight and pressure indicate a new treatment-phase risk.
review.anticipation: Watch for hypovolemia and electrolyte depletion during ongoing diuresis and communicate the trajectory before symptomatic deterioration.
review.uncertainty: The appropriate replacement fraction and duration require the patient’s current clinical and laboratory assessment.

context: A patient with type 1 diabetes is recovering from DKA after fluid and insulin treatment. Glucose is 180 mg/dL and blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is 0.4 mmol/L. Venous pH is 7.31, but bicarbonate remains 16 mmol/L. Chloride has risen after treatment and the anion gap is no longer elevated. The patient is alert and ready to eat. The team is reviewing transition from the intravenous pathway.
prompt: Which evaluation best supports the transition decision?

options.text: Use the closed anion gap as the sole endpoint and stop intravenous insulin before arranging further insulin coverage
options.explanation: The anion gap alone is not the preferred resolution endpoint, and type 1 diabetes requires an uninterrupted appropriate insulin plan during transition.

options.text: Repeat urine ketones and delay the transition until the urine test becomes negative
options.explanation: Urine ketones may remain positive or increase as beta-hydroxybutyrate converts during recovery. They can mislead when used as the resolution gate despite improving blood ketones and pH.

options.text: Review ketone and pH resolution, consider hyperchloremic acidosis and coordinate subcutaneous insulin coverage under protocol
options.explanation: Low blood ketones and pH above the consensus resolution threshold support resolution of ketoacidosis despite a residual bicarbonate reduction. Hyperchloremic acidosis can follow treatment; transition still requires a coordinated insulin plan and the full clinical review.

options.text: Continue the DKA pathway until bicarbonate reaches its target, treating the low value as proof of persistent ketogenesis
options.explanation: Bicarbonate alone may remain reduced from hyperchloremic acidosis after ketones resolve. It should not be treated as proof of ongoing ketogenesis when the ketone and pH endpoints support resolution.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

reasoning: Distinguish persistent ketoacidosis from a treatment-associated non-gap acidosis.
Evaluate resolution using the relevant metabolic endpoints.
Anticipate insulin gaps during transition despite apparent biochemical recovery.
review.debrief: Advanced evaluation asks why a residual abnormality persists. A value can remain outside its range for a different mechanism after the original emergency has resolved.
review.conflict: Bicarbonate remains low while blood ketones and pH support resolution, with rising chloride offering a competing explanation.
review.anticipation: Coordinate the protocol transition and subcutaneous insulin coverage to avoid recurrent ketosis or hypoglycemia.
review.uncertainty: The exact insulin regimen, timing and nutritional plan require the team’s individualized protocol review.

references.title: ADA 2026: diabetes care in the hospital

context: A bedbound adult with dark skin reports a newly sore heel. The heel feels warmer and firmer than the opposite side. The skin is intact and there is no obvious bright redness. The nurse is performing the scheduled skin assessment.
prompt: Which finding most supports concern for early pressure-related tissue damage?

options.text: Localized discomfort with a change in tissue temperature and firmness
options.explanation: These local tissue changes over a loaded heel warrant focused assessment and pressure relief. Visible redness is not required to recognize concern, particularly when skin color changes are subtle.

options.text: Intact skin without a clearly visible change in surface color
options.explanation: An intact surface does not exclude underlying pressure-related damage. Color alone is insufficient for assessment of this heel.

options.text: A generalized reduction in mobility during the hospital admission
options.explanation: Immobility explains exposure to pressure but is less specific than the new localized changes when judging this heel.

options.text: The absence of reported discomfort in the patient’s opposite heel
options.explanation: The comparison helps establish asymmetry but does not make the affected heel normal. The positive local findings require attention.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Increased warmth and firmness over a pressure area
Intact dark skin without obvious redness
reasoning: Recognize a meaningful tissue change without depending on visible redness.
review.debrief: Assess pain, temperature, consistency and skin appearance together. An intact surface and subtle color change do not eliminate the opportunity for early prevention.

context: The electronic chart lists a respiratory rate of 16/min. At the bedside the patient appears to be breathing much faster. The patient is sitting still and has not just exercised. The nurse is about to complete the current observation set.
prompt: Which action best establishes the current respiratory rate?

options.text: Use the monitor’s heart-rate trend to estimate the respiratory change.
options.explanation: Heart rate may change with respiratory illness but does not measure respiratory rate. It cannot resolve this discrepancy.

options.text: Repeat oxygen saturation and use that result to confirm the charted rate.
options.explanation: Oxygen saturation and respiratory rate measure different features. A reassuring saturation would not establish a normal breathing rate.

options.text: Ask the patient to breathe slowly before repeating the observation.
options.explanation: Coaching the pattern before counting changes the observation and can conceal the spontaneous abnormality that needs assessment.

options.text: Count and assess respirations directly, then record the observed finding.
options.explanation: A fresh direct observation resolves the discrepancy and allows assessment of depth, effort and pattern. A previous value or a different vital sign cannot substitute for the current rate.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: The charted respiratory rate conflicts with observed breathing.
The patient is resting without a recent exertional explanation.
reasoning: Resolve an observation discrepancy using the measurement that directly answers it.
review.debrief: Verify the variable in question. A normal reading from another device does not settle a conflicting bedside observation.

context: A red-cell transfusion began ten minutes ago. The patient now develops shaking chills and new back pain. Blood pressure is falling compared with the pre-transfusion value. The nurse is at the bedside with the emergency call system available.
prompt: Which immediate action best addresses a suspected serious transfusion reaction?

options.text: Stop the transfusion and flush the blood-filled tubing to preserve access.
options.explanation: Stopping is appropriate, but flushing the blood-filled line can deliver additional implicated blood. Maintain access using the institution’s reaction procedure.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and discard the component before beginning investigation.
options.explanation: The component and administration equipment may be required for investigation. Follow the local handling and notification process rather than discarding evidence.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and initiate urgent bedside assessment and help.
options.explanation: Interrupt the possible exposure while assessing airway, breathing and circulation and obtaining urgent assistance. Follow the reaction pathway, preserve the component for investigation and maintain access according to policy without flushing the blood-filled line.

options.text: Reduce the transfusion rate while obtaining a repeat observation set.
options.explanation: A serious reaction is possible; reducing the rate continues the exposure. Repeat observations are needed alongside stopping the transfusion.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: New chills and back pain shortly after transfusion starts
reasoning: Recognize a time-linked reaction and interrupt the possible exposure safely.
review.debrief: Immediate safety actions can begin before the reaction subtype is known. Stop exposure, assess severity and preserve the information needed for investigation.

references.title: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: suspected transfusion reactions

context: A hospitalized adult says they need the toilet now. They became dizzy during the previous transfer. Their call bell is outside their reach. The nurse is helping plan the next transfer.
prompt: Which plan best addresses the immediate need and transfer risk?

options.text: Complete the admission falls checklist before arranging the next toilet transfer.
options.explanation: Assessment is valuable, but the immediate need and known transfer difficulty already support assistance. A checklist should not create an avoidable delay.

options.text: Arrange timely assisted toileting and place the call bell within reach.
options.explanation: This responds to the need driving the attempted transfer while making assistance usable. The dizziness also requires assessment and an individualized mobility plan.

options.text: Provide the walking frame and ask the patient to transfer when dizziness settles.
options.explanation: A walking aid does not resolve the recent dizziness or the need for assistance during this transfer. Waiting without a practical toileting option may prompt an unassisted attempt.

options.text: Place a falls-risk sign and ask the patient to call before standing.
options.explanation: A sign and instruction do not help when the call bell remains unreachable. The immediate toileting need also remains unresolved.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Help is not reachable from bed
reasoning: Match a practical prevention measure to the current trigger and access barrier.
review.debrief: A prevention plan works when the patient can use it. Address the reason for movement, the transfer difficulty and the availability of help together.

references.title: NICE NG249: falls assessment and prevention

context: An adult has a deep forearm wound after a machinery injury. Blood is flowing continuously from the accessible wound. Emergency assistance has already been requested. Protective equipment and dressings are available.
prompt: Which action should begin while the emergency team arrives?

options.text: Apply firm direct pressure to the accessible bleeding wound.
options.explanation: Direct pressure addresses the immediate source of blood loss while assessment and emergency support continue. Further measures depend on bleeding control, injury and the trained team’s pathway.

options.text: Elevate the arm and assess whether the bleeding rate decreases.
options.explanation: Elevation does not provide the direct hemostatic control needed for continuous significant bleeding from an accessible wound.

options.text: Assess distal sensation and movement before applying a dressing.
options.explanation: Neurovascular examination is important, but controlling active significant bleeding should not await the full distal assessment.

options.text: Expose and irrigate the wound to identify the damaged vessel.
options.explanation: Irrigation and detailed exploration do not provide the immediate control required. Repeated manipulation can delay hemostasis.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

reasoning: Recognize an immediately controllable threat and select a direct response.
review.debrief: Control an accessible source of significant blood loss while the wider trauma assessment proceeds. Diagnostic detail should support timely action rather than delay it.

context: A postoperative patient’s respiratory rate has risen from 16 to 28/min over two hours. They are newly restless and cannot finish the same short walk as earlier. Blood pressure remains 124/76 mmHg. The patient says the pain is unchanged. The nurse is deciding which focused reassessment should lead the next review.
prompt: Which focused assessment takes priority for the new tachypnea and reduced walking tolerance?

options.text: Assess postoperative pain during movement and compare the current analgesic schedule with earlier doses.
options.explanation: Pain assessment is useful, but unchanged pain does not adequately account for the new respiratory and functional pattern. It should not displace breathing assessment.

options.text: Assess postural blood pressure and oral intake to determine whether the walking difficulty is volume-related.
options.explanation: Volume status may contribute, but positional testing does not first address tachypnea and restlessness. The patient needs current respiratory assessment rather than a narrow mobility explanation.

options.text: Assess leg strength and balance to revise the mobility-assistance level before the next walk.
options.explanation: A mobility assessment will help prevent harm but does not explain or address the evolving resting respiratory findings.

options.text: Assess work of breathing, oxygenation and the trajectory of symptoms while arranging prompt clinical review.
options.explanation: The respiratory and functional changes converge despite one reassuring vital sign. A focused breathing assessment and escalation address possible deterioration without assuming a specific pulmonary cause.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: A rising respiratory rate over two hours
Preserved blood pressure with unchanged pain
reasoning: Integrate respiratory and functional trends rather than weighting blood pressure alone.
Prioritize assessment of the system showing current deterioration.
review.debrief: A stable blood pressure does not make a changed patient stable. Use converging trends to decide which focused assessment and escalation are needed now.

context: An older adult became lightheaded and nearly fell during a morning transfer. A blood-pressure medicine was increased yesterday. The patient ate and drank little overnight. They feel better after sitting down. No injury or ongoing focal neurologic symptom is reported.
prompt: What should the next transfer plan address after the medication change and lightheaded near fall?

options.text: Provide a walking aid and attribute the episode to deconditioning unless resting pressure falls again.
options.explanation: A resting pressure does not reproduce postural physiology, and a walking aid does not resolve a potentially medication-related episode.

options.text: Provide bed rest for the day and ask the prescriber to reverse the medicine change without further assessment.
options.explanation: Restricting mobility and presuming a medication cause bypasses assessment of intake, observations and other contributors. The team needs evidence for an individualized treatment decision.

options.text: Provide supported transfers and review postural symptoms, observations, intake and the medication change with the team.
options.explanation: Timing suggests potentially interacting contributors to postural symptoms. Supported mobility prevents another fall while assessment and medication review clarify the cause rather than assigning it to a single factor.

options.text: Provide extra oral fluids and repeat an unassisted transfer to determine whether the dizziness has resolved.
options.explanation: Reduced intake may matter, but it does not establish the cause or justify testing recovery through another unassisted near-fall opportunity.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Symptoms occurred during a transfer and improved when seated.
A blood-pressure medicine was increased yesterday.
reasoning: Connect symptom timing with recent treatment and intake changes.
Combine immediate transfer support with an assessment that can distinguish contributors.
review.debrief: Prevent the next fall while investigating why the episode occurred. A plausible cause is a hypothesis to assess, rather than a reason to stop considering the rest of the clinical context.

references.title: NICE NG249: falls assessment and prevention

context: A patient is unusually quiet and loses track of a conversation this afternoon. Their daughter says they were attentive and managing their own medicines yesterday. The admission note mentions chronic memory difficulty. The patient’s temperature is within the reference range. The nurse is reviewing whether this represents a change from baseline.
prompt: Which interpretation should guide the next assessment?

options.text: Use the normal temperature to prioritize sleep disruption before investigating medical contributors.
options.explanation: Delirium can arise without fever, and a normal temperature does not establish a benign explanation. Sleep and environmental factors should be assessed alongside medical causes.

options.text: Treat the recent change as possible delirium and assess contributors using the collateral baseline.
options.explanation: A chronic memory label and absence of fever do not explain away an acute change in attention and function. Use the local delirium assessment process and evaluate underlying causes and deterioration.

options.text: Use the chronic memory note as the baseline and focus on repeated orientation during the next shift.
options.explanation: The note does not resolve the reported acute difference. Orientation support may help, but accepting the historical label risks missing a current illness.

options.text: Use the daughter’s report to exclude chronic impairment and classify the change as an acute infection.
options.explanation: Collateral history supports acute change but does not establish the cause or exclude underlying chronic impairment. Infection is one possibility among several.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: New inattention and reduced engagement this afternoon
A relative describes intact function yesterday.
The record contains a chronic memory label.
reasoning: Compare current attention and function with a recent collateral baseline.
Keep acute medical causes open despite a chronic label and reassuring temperature.
review.debrief: A historical diagnosis is not a substitute for a current baseline comparison. Recognize acute changes in attention and behavior, including quiet presentations, and investigate their causes.

context: An incontinent patient has diffuse superficial irritation across skin exposed to urine. A separate painful area over the sacrum remains discolored after pressure is relieved. The patient has spent most of the day in bed. Barrier care was documented this morning. The nurse is deciding how to reassess the two areas.
prompt: Which assessment best explains the different prevention needs?

options.text: Assess moisture injury and pressure-related damage separately, then address both exposures in the care plan.
options.explanation: The distribution and persistent focal change suggest that more than one mechanism may be present. Barrier care can help moisture exposure without resolving sacral pressure loading.

options.text: Classify both areas as moisture damage because incontinence explains the skin’s prolonged exposure.
options.explanation: Moisture is relevant but does not adequately explain the separate persistent focal change over a loaded bony area.

options.text: Classify both areas as pressure damage because the patient has remained in bed most of the day.
options.explanation: Immobility increases risk but does not remove the need to distinguish diffuse moisture irritation from focal pressure damage.

options.text: Judge the response by whether the barrier product reduces visible irritation at the next application.
options.explanation: A moisture intervention’s surface response cannot establish whether the sacral loading problem has been addressed. Both areas and exposures need reassessment.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: A distinct painful area lies over the sacrum.
The sacral change persists after pressure relief.
The patient is mostly bedbound despite barrier care.
reasoning: Use location, tissue findings and exposure to distinguish potentially coexisting mechanisms.
Match reassessment and prevention to each mechanism rather than selecting one label for all changes.
review.debrief: Clinical reasoning can support more than one explanation at once. A single successful intervention does not establish that every cause of tissue harm has been addressed.

context: A patient receiving red cells develops new breathlessness after 45 minutes. Oxygen saturation falls from 96% to 89% on the same oxygen setting. The patient has chronic heart failure and says this feels like a previous fluid episode. There is no rash or recorded fever. The transfusion is still running when the nurse arrives.
prompt: Which response best prioritizes the new respiratory change?

options.text: Reduce the transfusion rate and request a diuretic because the history favors fluid intolerance.
options.explanation: Fluid overload is plausible, but reducing the rate continues the exposure and selects a mechanism before urgent reaction assessment. The initial safety response should not depend on proving the subtype.

options.text: Increase oxygen and use the next saturation to decide whether the transfusion should be interrupted.
options.explanation: Oxygen support is appropriate but a transient numerical improvement would not make continued exposure safe during an unexplained new respiratory reaction.

options.text: Pause the transfusion and restart at a slower rate once the patient reports less breathlessness.
options.explanation: A subjective response does not identify the cause or establish safe re-exposure after respiratory compromise. Restart decisions require the appropriate clinical review and policy.

options.text: Stop the transfusion, support and assess breathing, and activate the urgent reaction-review pathway.
options.explanation: A serious transfusion-associated complication is possible. Interrupt exposure and assess severity before assuming fluid overload or excluding a reaction because rash and fever are absent.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Saturation has fallen on unchanged oxygen.
Heart failure provides a plausible fluid-related explanation.
There is no rash or recorded fever.
reasoning: Connect the timing of respiratory deterioration to a possible transfusion-associated event.
Prioritize interruption and assessment before choosing a specific causal treatment.
review.debrief: A familiar comorbidity can supply a plausible explanation without settling the cause. Begin the safety pathway while the team distinguishes the relevant mechanisms.

references.title: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: suspected transfusion reactions

context: A patient is reassessed after a road collision. Initial focused ultrasound showed no free intraperitoneal fluid. Over 30 minutes heart rate rises and blood pressure falls despite initial resuscitation. The patient develops pelvic and lower-back pain, while external bleeding is controlled. An early hemoglobin result is near baseline. The trauma team is returning to the bedside.
prompt: Which cause of circulatory deterioration requires renewed investigation despite the negative FAST and early hemoglobin?

options.text: The pelvic pain establishes the bleeding source, so further reassessment should focus on that region during resuscitation.
options.explanation: The pelvis is important, but pain does not establish the sole source or exclude additional injuries and causes. Reassessment should prioritize likely sources without prematurely narrowing the whole evaluation.

options.text: The initially stable hemoglobin favors pain-related tachycardia, so analgesic response should determine the urgency of investigation.
options.explanation: Pain can increase heart rate, but falling pressure despite initial resuscitation requires a broader urgent assessment. An analgesic response would not exclude concealed blood loss.

options.text: Possible concealed hemorrhage requires renewed source assessment and team-directed investigation matched to current stability.
options.explanation: A negative FAST cannot exclude all intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding, and an early hemoglobin can lag acute loss. The worsening circulation and pain warrant urgent reassessment without relying on either reassuring test to close the hemorrhage pathway.

options.text: A negative FAST shifts priority toward medication-related hypotension while repeat blood counts clarify whether bleeding exists.
options.explanation: Medication effects can contribute, but the changing physiology and injury pattern already support urgent hemorrhage reassessment. Waiting for a hemoglobin fall gives an early test too much exclusionary weight.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Worsening hemodynamic trend despite initial resuscitation
reasoning: Reconcile the limitations of early imaging and hemoglobin with the evolving clinical pattern.
Prioritize concealed hemorrhage while keeping a team-directed pathway appropriate to current stability.
review.debrief: Evaluate negative tests in relation to their scope and timing. A worsening patient can require a renewed hemorrhage pathway before a previously reassuring test becomes abnormal.
review.conflict: Initial ultrasound and hemoglobin appear reassuring, but circulation is worsening and pain suggests a possible concealed injury.
review.anticipation: Anticipate further circulatory collapse and prepare for a stability-dependent diagnostic and hemostatic response with the trauma team.
review.uncertainty: The information does not establish the bleeding site or show that transfer for a particular imaging test is safe.

context: An older adult taking an anticoagulant is observed after a head injury. An earlier CT was reported without an acute bleed. Three hours later the patient vomits twice and becomes harder to keep awake. Their GCS falls from 15 to 13 on repeat assessment. Blood pressure and oxygen saturation remain near baseline. An opioid was given before the change, creating another possible explanation.
prompt: How should the new vomiting and GCS decline be evaluated after an earlier CT without an acute bleed?

options.text: Prioritize anticoagulation-reversal preparation as a confirmed bleed and defer the medication assessment to the receiving team.
options.explanation: Urgent review and preparation may be needed, but the nurse cannot infer a confirmed bleed or an independent reversal decision from these findings. Assessing drug effects can occur alongside evaluation of injury complications.

options.text: Urgently escalate the neurologic decline and reassess head-injury complications and drug effects in parallel.
options.explanation: An earlier CT and stable peripheral observations do not settle a new neurologic change. Recent opioid exposure is relevant but must not prevent urgent reassessment for intracranial deterioration and a team decision about further investigation.

options.text: Use the recent opioid as the working explanation and let improved arousal determine whether head-injury review is needed.
options.explanation: Drug effect is plausible, but using its response as a gate to injury review risks missing a concurrent complication. The repeated vomiting and documented GCS decline already warrant escalation.

options.text: Repeat routine observations and request another scan if pressure or saturation begins to depart from baseline.
options.explanation: Normal pressure and oxygenation do not exclude neurologic deterioration. These are not appropriate prerequisites for escalation of a documented fall in GCS.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Earlier CT without an acute bleed
Preserved pressure and saturation with recent opioid exposure
reasoning: Give a new neurologic trend appropriate weight despite prior negative imaging.
Evaluate medication and injury mechanisms concurrently without requiring a peripheral vital-sign change.
review.debrief: Reassessment tests whether the patient’s current trajectory fits the previous conclusion. A plausible drug effect does not cancel a time-sensitive injury differential.
review.conflict: The earlier CT and recent opioid favor reassurance or sedation, while repeated vomiting and a measured GCS decline indicate potentially serious change.
review.anticipation: Anticipate further loss of airway protection and prepare for urgent team-directed reassessment and investigation.
review.uncertainty: The findings establish deterioration, but do not distinguish drug effect, intracranial injury or combined causes.

context: A transfusion has been stopped because a patient developed acute hypoxemia. They have bilateral crackles and a new bilateral chest opacity. There is chronic kidney disease and a positive fluid balance. The patient is also febrile and blood pressure has fallen. An elevated natriuretic peptide was recorded before transfusion, so its interpretation is limited. The responding team is evaluating the pulmonary complication.
prompt: What should guide distinction between pulmonary transfusion-reaction mechanisms in this patient?

options.text: Compare circulatory overload, lung injury and other reaction mechanisms using timing, baseline data and current findings.
options.explanation: Several transfusion complications can produce hypoxemia and bilateral opacities. Fluid exposure supports overload, while fever and hypotension require broader assessment; a biomarker already elevated before the event cannot independently establish the cause.

options.text: Treat the positive balance and elevated biomarker as sufficient evidence of overload and use diuretic response to confirm it.
options.explanation: Those findings support a hypothesis but do not settle the competing features or exclude other mechanisms. A treatment response should not substitute for the appropriate urgent reaction investigation.

options.text: Treat fever and low pressure as sufficient evidence of lung injury and exclude fluid exposure from the working assessment.
options.explanation: Fever and hypotension can occur with several serious reactions. Ignoring fluid exposure discards relevant evidence and incorrectly converts suggestive findings into a confirmed subtype.

options.text: Use the pre-transfusion biomarker to establish chronic congestion and classify the new oxygen decline as expected baseline disease.
options.explanation: The biomarker’s baseline elevation limits its discriminatory value; it does not explain away a new oxygen requirement and new imaging findings during transfusion.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Kidney disease and positive fluid balance
An elevated biomarker preceded the event
reasoning: Identify evidence shared by several pulmonary reaction mechanisms and assess its specificity.
Use baseline comparisons and discordant current findings to guide continued investigation rather than a premature subtype label.
review.debrief: A useful advanced synthesis explains why the obvious diagnosis remains uncertain. Identify which findings discriminate, which are shared and which were present before the event.
review.conflict: Fluid risk supports overload, while fever and falling pressure broaden the differential; the biomarker was abnormal before the event.
review.anticipation: Continue respiratory and hemodynamic reassessment and the reaction investigation while the team determines mechanism-specific treatment.
review.uncertainty: The scenario does not establish TACO, TRALI, sepsis or another reaction subtype, and more than one mechanism may contribute.

references.title: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: suspected transfusion reactions

context: A patient’s heel remains intact after a pressure-relief plan was introduced. Recorded repositioning tasks are complete, and the visible color appears unchanged. The patient reports increasing deep heel pain and the tissue feels more boggy. They have lost weight and are eating poorly. During assessment the heel is resting against the mattress despite the documented offloading plan. The team is deciding whether prevention has been effective.
prompt: Which evaluation should determine whether the heel offloading plan has actually worked?

options.text: Use the completed turning record to confirm pressure relief and prioritize a new support surface for persistent pain.
options.explanation: A different support surface may help, but the record does not establish effective heel offloading. The heel is observed to remain loaded, so actual delivery and local tissue findings need reassessment before relying on the turning record.

options.text: Use the weight loss to make nutrition supplementation the main intervention before revising the pressure-relief method.
options.explanation: Nutrition risk is important, but it does not remove the immediate need to address ongoing heel loading and worsening local findings. The two contributors should be managed together.

options.text: Use unchanged surface color as evidence of stability and increase analgesia while checking offloading at the next scheduled turn.
options.explanation: Color alone does not establish tissue stability. Increasing pain, bogginess and observed loading call for reassessment now rather than treating pain as an isolated symptom.

options.text: Reassess tissue and actual offloading effectiveness, revise the plan and address the contributing nutrition risk.
options.explanation: Documentation and surface appearance do not establish that loading was relieved or tissue injury prevented. Worsening pain and consistency plus observed loading require assessment and plan revision, while nutrition risk needs appropriate review.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Intact heel with unchanged visible color
The heel is still loaded despite the plan
reasoning: Separate documented task completion from actual delivery and patient outcome.
Integrate tissue changes, ongoing loading and nutrition risk to revise the prevention plan.
review.debrief: Evaluate the patient and the intervention as delivered. A completed checklist can coexist with a failed prevention mechanism and a worsening outcome.
review.conflict: Completed tasks and an intact surface suggest success, while worsening deep findings and observed heel loading suggest ineffective prevention.
review.anticipation: Recheck the revised offloading method in use and track local tissue findings, comfort and relevant nutrition follow-up.
review.uncertainty: The information does not establish the depth or stage of injury; specialist tissue assessment may be needed.

context: A patient with mild chronic cognitive impairment becomes unusually sleepy and stops eating lunch. A family member describes independent conversation and eating at breakfast. Routine temperature and blood pressure remain near baseline. A sedating medicine was added last night, and urine output has fallen today. The patient briefly answers orientation questions correctly but loses attention during the conversation. The nurse is deciding whether the current observation score explains the concern.
prompt: How should the acute sleepiness and inattention be evaluated despite a reassuring routine observation score?

options.text: Use the new sedating medicine to establish a drug effect and defer other investigation until the dose is reviewed.
options.explanation: The medicine is a relevant hypothesis but does not explain all current findings or exclude another concurrent cause. Reduced output and acute functional change warrant a broader assessment now.

options.text: Use the chronic cognitive diagnosis to prioritize behavioral support and reserve escalation for a higher observation score.
options.explanation: A chronic diagnosis cannot define this patient’s current baseline, and a score may miss clinically important attention and functional changes. Clinical concern can justify escalation before the score rises.

options.text: Escalate the acute functional and attention change and assess medication, perfusion and other delirium contributors together.
options.explanation: The acute change and fluctuation remain important despite correct brief orientation and stable routine values. Medication effects, organ dysfunction and other causes require assessment without attributing the whole pattern to the chronic label or a single new treatment.

options.text: Use the correct orientation responses to favor ordinary fatigue and repeat the same observations after uninterrupted rest.
options.explanation: Brief orientation does not resolve fluctuating attention or the documented functional decline. Rest may help, but it should not delay assessment of possible acute illness and reduced output.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: A clear change from breakfast function
Fluctuating attention despite brief correct orientation
reasoning: Compare the current function and attention with a recent person-specific baseline.
Integrate medication exposure and organ findings while recognizing the limits of routine scoring.
Prioritize evaluation of an acute change without presuming a single cause.
review.debrief: Clinical concern can precede an abnormal score. Advanced reasoning uses collateral function, attention and organ trends to recognize a changed patient and keep several plausible causes under review.
review.conflict: Near-baseline routine observations and brief correct orientation contrast with clear acute functional decline and fluctuating attention.
review.anticipation: Reassess consciousness, intake, output and safety while the team identifies contributors and evaluates response to its plan.
review.uncertainty: The information supports urgent assessment of acute change, but does not establish delirium’s cause or an independent medication change.

context: An adult receives a hereditary cancer panel report. The report lists a variant of uncertain significance. The patient asks whether this means the variant causes cancer. The nurse is preparing the initial explanation before the genetics appointment.
prompt: How should the nurse explain the variant of uncertain significance?

options.text: The evidence does not yet establish whether this variant changes cancer risk.
options.explanation: An uncertain classification means the available evidence cannot establish the variant as harmful or benign. It does not independently establish a hereditary cancer diagnosis or replace assessment of the person and family history.

options.text: The panel found an inherited cause that explains the patient’s cancer risk.
options.explanation: This converts an uncertain finding into a pathogenic result. Detecting a sequence change is different from establishing that the change causes disease.

options.text: The panel excludes inherited risk because the variant was not called pathogenic.
options.explanation: An uncertain finding is not a definitive negative result. Other genetic or familial risk may remain, depending on test coverage and history.

options.text: The result establishes carrier status without implications for the patient’s own health.
options.explanation: Carrier status has a specific relationship to the gene and inheritance pattern. An uncertain classification alone does not support that interpretation.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: The laboratory classified the finding as a variant of uncertain significance.
The patient equates the result with a disease-causing variant.
reasoning: Distinguish detection of a variant from evidence that it causes disease.
review.debrief: Interpret the laboratory classification before assigning clinical meaning. An uncertain result calls for accurate explanation and planned review, rather than certainty in either direction.

references.title: NCI: genetic testing for inherited cancer risk

context: A patient says several relatives have had cancer. The intake form contains names but no cancer diagnoses. The ages at diagnosis have not been recorded. The nurse has time for one focused clarification before the consultation.
prompt: Which clarification provides the most useful information for hereditary-risk assessment?

options.text: Record the total number of relatives affected and their current ages together.
options.explanation: A family count is incomplete without the relationship and diagnosis, and current age cannot substitute for age at diagnosis.

options.text: Record the relatives’ treatments and whether each person tolerated chemotherapy well.
options.explanation: Treatment history can later clarify a diagnosis, but treatment tolerance is less useful than the missing relationship, diagnosis and age information for this initial risk assessment.

options.text: Record the relatives’ shared diet and smoking history before expanding the pedigree.
options.explanation: Shared exposures can matter, but they do not replace the missing basic family-history elements needed to assess an inherited pattern.

options.text: Record each affected relative’s biological relationship, cancer diagnosis and age at diagnosis.
options.explanation: Relationship, cancer type and age at diagnosis help identify patterns that may warrant more detailed genetic assessment. A list of names or a broad count does not provide those distinctions.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Several relatives reportedly had cancer without a documented diagnosis.
reasoning: Identify the missing history elements that determine an inherited pattern.
review.debrief: A useful family history connects the diagnosis to a biological relationship and timing. Collect those basic elements before drawing conclusions about inheritance.

references.title: CDC: family health history and adults

context: A patient brings a report from sequencing of a removed tumor. The report identifies a change that may guide cancer treatment. No blood or saliva testing for inherited variants has been performed. The patient asks whether the tumor result proves that a sibling has the same change.
prompt: Which response best distinguishes the two types of testing?

options.text: Explain that tumor findings concern acquired changes and exclude inherited family implications.
options.explanation: Some tumor findings prompt germline assessment. Excluding inherited implications solely because the original sample was tumor tissue closes that evaluation too early.

options.text: Explain that the sibling should use the tumor result to select a surveillance schedule.
options.explanation: A sibling’s surveillance depends on that person’s risk assessment and any appropriately established familial variant. Acting directly on another person’s tumor report skips this distinction.

options.text: Explain that a tumor finding may need separate inherited-risk evaluation before family conclusions.
options.explanation: Tumor changes may be acquired in the tumor or may reflect an inherited finding. The tumor report alone does not establish a sibling’s genotype; the treating and genetics teams determine whether germline evaluation is appropriate.

options.text: Explain that a treatment-relevant tumor change establishes a shared inherited family variant.
options.explanation: A treatment target in tumor tissue is not automatically an inherited variant. Family conclusions require the appropriate inherited-risk assessment.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: The sample was tumor tissue used to guide treatment.
No inherited-variant test has been performed.
The patient wants to infer a sibling’s result.
reasoning: Distinguish a tumor-specific treatment finding from an established inherited variant.
review.debrief: Identify what sample was tested and what the test was designed to answer. A report that guides one patient’s treatment may raise a family question without answering it.

references.title: NCI: genetic testing for inherited cancer risk

context: A competent adult attends a genetic-testing appointment. The patient says a relative booked the test and expects it to be completed today. The patient says they do not understand what the result could mean. A sample kit is ready on the desk.
prompt: What is the nurse’s best next step before collecting the sample?

options.text: Use the signed appointment form to confirm consent and proceed with specimen collection.
options.explanation: An administrative form does not resolve the patient’s stated lack of understanding. Consent is a process, rather than an inference from attendance or paperwork.

options.text: Pause collection and arrange an explanation of benefits, limits and the patient’s testing preferences.
options.explanation: Voluntary informed consent requires the patient’s understanding and choice. A ready kit and family expectation do not replace discussion of benefits, limitations, consequences and whether the person wants testing.

options.text: Collect the sample and schedule a detailed explanation when the result becomes available.
options.explanation: Explaining a result later cannot substitute for informed choice before testing. Collection should follow an adequate consent process.

options.text: Ask the relative to explain the expected benefit and confirm the patient’s testing plan.
options.explanation: Family input may be helpful with permission, but the competent adult’s understanding and preferences must direct consent. A relative cannot supply these on the patient’s behalf.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: The patient does not understand the potential meaning of the test.
A relative expects the test to proceed today.
reasoning: Recognize that stated lack of understanding requires a consent discussion before testing.
review.debrief: Treat the patient’s expressed uncertainty as a consent issue. Support a voluntary decision before completing the technical steps of testing.

references.title: MedlinePlus Genetics: informed consent for genetic testing

context: A patient reads that a gene is associated with the response to a prescribed medicine. The patient has not had a clinical pharmacogenetic test. They ask whether the association means they should halve their dose tonight. The nurse is responding to this question during medication teaching.
prompt: Which guidance best addresses the patient’s interpretation?

options.text: Continue the prescribed plan while the prescriber or pharmacist reviews whether testing affects this medicine.
options.explanation: An association does not establish this patient’s genotype, a need for routine testing or an individual dose change. Medication decisions require the relevant evidence, labeling and clinical context with the prescribing team.

options.text: Reduce the dose temporarily because a gene association predicts reduced metabolism in most patients.
options.explanation: The association does not identify this person’s metabolism or support a temporary dose reduction. An unnecessary reduction can compromise treatment.

options.text: Request a broad commercial panel and use its dose suggestions before the next prescription review.
options.explanation: Test scope, clinical validity and the relevant medication must be considered before using a report to guide therapy. A broad panel is not a substitute for a supervised medication review.

options.text: Reassure the patient that a tolerated medicine is unaffected by inherited differences in metabolism.
options.explanation: Prior tolerance does not establish the absence of a pharmacogenetic effect. The appropriate response is review, without unsupported reassurance or an independent dose change.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: A published gene–drug association is not an individual clinical test result.
The patient proposes changing the prescribed dose.
reasoning: Distinguish a population association from an individual medication instruction.
review.debrief: Genetic information needs interpretation within the medication plan. Avoid translating an association into a dose change without the patient-specific evidence and prescribing review.

context: An unaffected adult has a negative hereditary cancer panel. A sibling had colorectal cancer at age 38 but has not had genetic testing. The family has no previously identified pathogenic variant. The patient asks to cancel enhanced surveillance planned from the family history. The nurse is preparing the follow-up discussion.
prompt: How should the negative panel affect the plan to cancel family-history-based surveillance?

options.text: Use the negative panel to return to routine surveillance and revisit genetics if another relative is diagnosed.
options.explanation: This treats an uninformative negative as a true negative and discounts the existing early-onset diagnosis. Waiting for another family diagnosis is not a sound reason to abandon the current history-based plan.

options.text: Repeat the same panel in the unaffected patient before deciding whether the surveillance plan is necessary.
options.explanation: Repeating an unchanged test is less informative than reviewing its scope and considering the affected sibling. It also makes a new test a prerequisite for a risk discussion already supported by history.

options.text: Treat the sibling’s early diagnosis as evidence of a familial variant and arrange variant testing for other relatives.
options.explanation: The history warrants assessment but does not establish a specific pathogenic variant. Targeted family testing requires an appropriately identified familial finding.

options.text: Maintain the history-based plan pending genetics review of the result and possible testing of the affected sibling.
options.explanation: Without an established familial variant, a negative panel can be uninformative. Review should integrate the pedigree and test scope; testing an affected relative may clarify the family’s risk without treating the current result as an all-clear.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: A sibling developed colorectal cancer at age 38.
No familial pathogenic variant has been identified.
The patient plans to stop history-based surveillance after a negative panel.
reasoning: Determine whether the negative test can be interpreted against a known familial variant.
Integrate unresolved family risk with surveillance and the most informative next assessment.
review.debrief: A negative result has meaning in relation to what the test could detect. Use the family history and the presence or absence of an established familial variant to guide follow-up.

references.title: NCI: genetic testing for inherited cancer risk
CDC: family health history and adults

context: An adult arrives for predictive testing with a parent. The parent answers most questions and says testing must happen before a family event next week. The patient quietly tells the nurse that they want time to consider the result’s implications. The sample has not been collected. The patient has decision-making capacity.
prompt: How should the nurse proceed when the patient wants more time but the parent expects testing today?

options.text: Collect the sample today and hold its release while the patient considers whether they want the result.
options.explanation: This advances the testing process before resolving the patient’s choice. With no specimen collected, a private consent discussion is more appropriate than creating a new release decision.

options.text: Use the approaching family event to agree a testing date and address privacy concerns after collection.
options.explanation: A family deadline does not determine the patient’s readiness. The expressed wish for time should be addressed before committing to collection or disclosure.

options.text: Offer a private discussion, clarify the patient’s preferences and arrange a later decision if desired.
options.explanation: A private conversation helps establish the patient’s own understanding and voluntary choice in the presence of family pressure. Testing can be deferred while preserving access to counseling and family involvement chosen by the patient.

options.text: Complete counseling with both people and ask the parent to confirm that the patient is ready for testing.
options.explanation: A family discussion can be useful, but parent confirmation does not establish the competent adult’s voluntary consent and may reinforce the pressure already described.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: The parent is directing the conversation.
A family event creates pressure to test this week.
The competent patient wants more time.
reasoning: Recognize the difference between supportive family involvement and pressure on consent.
Prioritize private clarification of the patient’s choice before specimen collection.
review.debrief: Person-centered genetic care includes control over whether and when to test. Resolve pressure and understanding before proceeding with a technically convenient plan.

references.title: MedlinePlus Genetics: informed consent for genetic testing

context: A patient had an uncertain variant reported three years ago. The original report recommended periodic review through the genetics service. A first-degree relative has now developed a related cancer at an unusually young age. The patient has not contacted the genetics team since the original result. They ask whether the old report still settles the issue.
prompt: What follow-up is needed after a new early-onset family cancer and an older uncertain result?

options.text: Order the same panel again before requesting review so the genetics team has a recent specimen result.
options.explanation: A new specimen is not automatically needed to review classification, test coverage or family data. Reviewing the existing report and updated history should determine the appropriate next test, if any.

options.text: Update the pedigree and request genetics review of the current classification, test scope and family findings.
options.explanation: New family information and possible laboratory reclassification can change interpretation and follow-up needs. Updating the history and reviewing the actual report are more useful than presuming either a pathogenic result or a permanently settled uncertainty.

options.text: Treat the new diagnosis as confirmation that the uncertain variant is pathogenic and update relatives’ risk labels.
options.explanation: A related cancer increases concern but does not establish variant pathogenicity. Classification requires appropriate evidence and review rather than a direct inference from one new diagnosis.

options.text: Use the original uncertain classification until the laboratory sends an unsolicited amended report.
options.explanation: This relies on outdated information despite a planned review and an important pedigree change. Recontact can be appropriate even without an unsolicited laboratory notice.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: The original variant classification was uncertain.
The report is three years old and recommended review.
A close relative has a new early-onset diagnosis.
There has been no genetics follow-up.
reasoning: Recognize that variant classification and family history may change over time.
Choose a coordinated update that determines whether additional testing or surveillance changes are warranted.
review.debrief: Follow-up is an information-management task as well as a testing task. New diagnoses and older uncertain reports should trigger review of the evidence rather than automatic reclassification or reflex repeat testing.

references.title: NCI: genetic testing for inherited cancer risk
CDC: family health history and adults

context: A patient reports that a cousin has a cancer gene. A screenshot shows the gene name but omits the variant and classification. The patient has been offered a broad direct-to-consumer test by a friend. A genetics visit is scheduled next month. They ask which result the clinical team needs to plan useful testing.
prompt: Which record is most important before choosing a test for the reported familial finding?

options.text: With permission, obtain the relative’s clinical report showing the exact variant and classification for genetics review.
options.explanation: The exact familial finding and its classification determine whether targeted clinical testing is appropriate. A gene name alone does not identify the variant or establish that a consumer test includes it.

options.text: Obtain the consumer test’s overall cancer-risk score and compare it with the cousin’s gene name.
options.explanation: An overall consumer score cannot substitute for verifying a specific clinical familial variant. The tests may measure different things and have different coverage.

options.text: Obtain a fresh blood sample for the broadest available panel before the genetics appointment.
options.explanation: A broader panel is not automatically the most informative next step. Clarifying the family’s actual finding can guide targeted testing and reduce uncertain findings.

options.text: Obtain the cousin’s surveillance schedule and use it to choose the patient’s testing pathway.
options.explanation: The cousin’s plan may reflect personal disease, a specific variant or other risk factors. It cannot replace confirming the actual report and assessing this patient’s history.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: The reported familial finding is based on an incomplete screenshot.
The variant and classification are missing.
The proposed consumer test may have different coverage.
A genetics consultation is already planned.
reasoning: Identify what evidence is missing from the reported family result.
Prioritize verification of the familial finding before selecting a testing strategy.
review.debrief: A reported gene name is a starting point, not a complete familial diagnosis. Verify the exact clinical finding and test coverage before translating another person’s result into this patient’s plan.

references.title: NCI: genetic testing for inherited cancer risk

context: A patient brings a pharmacogenetic report to a medication visit. The report flags a currently prescribed drug for clinician review. The patient began another medicine last week and now reports dizziness. They have not changed either dose. The nurse must decide what information to bring to the prescriber and pharmacist.
prompt: What information should guide the review of dizziness after the new medicine was started?

options.text: Review the flagged gene–drug pair first and attribute the dizziness to reduced metabolism of that drug.
options.explanation: This narrows the explanation before considering the newly added medicine and other clinical findings. A genetic association does not prove that it caused this symptom.

options.text: Review the new medicine as the cause and keep the genetic report for the next scheduled annual visit.
options.explanation: The new medicine is relevant, but excluding the report without review discards potentially useful information. Both medication changes and genetic evidence should be considered in the current assessment.

options.text: Review whether the patient tolerated the flagged drug previously and use that history to clear the interaction concern.
options.explanation: Prior tolerance does not resolve a new interaction or current symptoms. The current medicine combination and patient condition may differ from the earlier stable period.

options.text: Review the exact report, complete medication list, symptom timing and relevant clinical observations together.
options.explanation: The report may inform therapy, but interactions, timing and the current examination also affect the explanation for dizziness. An integrated review supports an appropriate prescribing decision without assuming a genetic cause.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: A clinical pharmacogenetic report flags a prescribed medicine.
Another medicine was added last week.
The prescribed doses have not been independently changed.
reasoning: Integrate the timing of symptoms with medication changes and the genetic report.
Prepare a supervised review that tests competing explanations rather than attributing the symptom to one finding.
review.debrief: Pharmacogenetics adds evidence to medication assessment. It does not replace symptom evaluation, medication reconciliation or attention to a recent change in treatment.

context: A 42-year-old has a negative hereditary cancer panel without an established familial variant. Their sibling developed colorectal cancer at 38. Over six weeks the patient has developed intermittent rectal bleeding, changed bowel habits and unintentional weight loss. Hemoglobin has fallen from 13.1 to 10.2 g/dL, although blood pressure is stable and there is no brisk current bleeding. A stool FIT obtained last month was below the local referral threshold. A genetics appointment is six weeks away, and the patient asks to postpone further assessment until that visit.
prompt: How should the new symptoms change the timing and purpose of follow-up while inherited risk remains unresolved?

options.text: Expedite an expanded hereditary panel so its result can determine the next diagnostic investigation.
options.explanation: The current symptoms require assessment irrespective of whether another inherited variant is found. Expanding a risk test does not diagnose or exclude the present cause of bleeding and anemia.

options.text: Bring forward routine risk-based surveillance and reassess the bleeding once that surveillance pathway is scheduled.
options.explanation: Moving surveillance earlier may sound responsive, but the current symptom cluster needs a diagnostic review with an appropriate urgency decision. Screening and surveillance schedules do not substitute for assessment of a new symptomatic problem.

options.text: Arrange prompt symptom-directed clinical assessment while keeping inherited-risk review on a separate pathway.
options.explanation: Persistent bleeding, changed bowel habits, weight loss and falling hemoglobin need diagnostic assessment of the current problem. A negative hereditary panel does not exclude sporadic disease, and a below-threshold FIT does not resolve strong concern from ongoing unexplained symptoms. The genetics review remains useful but should not delay this assessment.

options.text: Request repeat stool and iron studies as prerequisites to referral while addressing likely iron deficiency.
options.explanation: Additional studies can contribute, but making them a gate to clinical review delays assessment of a persistent concerning symptom cluster. A prior below-threshold result is not sufficient reassurance when clinical concern remains.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: Negative hereditary panel without a known familial variant
A sibling had early-onset colorectal cancer.
Persistent rectal bleeding and changed bowel habits
Falling hemoglobin despite preserved blood pressure
An earlier stool FIT below the local threshold
The patient proposes waiting six weeks for a genetics visit.
reasoning: Distinguish inherited-risk assessment and surveillance from diagnosis of a current symptomatic problem.
Weigh persistent symptoms and a hemoglobin trend against negative or below-threshold tests that answer more limited questions.
Prioritize diagnostic clinical review without abandoning the separate inherited-risk follow-up.
review.debrief: Advanced reasoning identifies when the clinical question has changed. A test about inherited susceptibility and a prior stool result cannot settle a new symptomatic presentation with a worsening blood-count trend.
review.conflict: Negative genetic testing, an earlier below-threshold FIT and stable pressure appear reassuring, while persistent symptoms, weight loss and falling hemoglobin sustain concern.
review.anticipation: Ensure the symptomatic referral is acted on and provide a team-agreed safety net for increasing bleeding, faintness or further deterioration while assessment proceeds.
review.uncertainty: These findings do not establish cancer or an inherited syndrome; they establish a need for diagnostic assessment rather than reassurance from risk tests.

context: A patient with a strong family history receives a variant of uncertain significance. An online discussion describes the same gene as a high-risk cancer gene. The patient requests an irreversible risk-reducing procedure because of the report. Their family-history risk assessment is not yet complete. No pathogenic familial variant has been established. The surgeon asks the nurse to clarify the patient’s understanding before multidisciplinary review.
prompt: Which assessment should precede a risk-reducing procedure requested because of this uncertain variant?

options.text: Repeat testing in another laboratory and base the procedural discussion on whether the same variant is detected again.
options.explanation: Repeated detection confirms presence, not pathogenicity. A second report does not replace variant interpretation or assessment of the patient’s independent risk.

options.text: Assess history-based risk and patient preferences with the team, separating that assessment from the uncertain variant.
options.explanation: The gene’s association does not establish this variant as disease-causing. The team should assess independent risk and the procedure’s benefits and harms with the patient; the uncertain variant alone should not determine the irreversible intervention.

options.text: Use the gene’s established association to support the procedure while the laboratory gathers variant-level evidence.
options.explanation: A gene-level association cannot substitute for evidence about this particular variant. Acting on that inference can expose the patient to irreversible harm without the required risk assessment.

options.text: Use the uncertain classification to defer the risk discussion until the laboratory upgrades or downgrades the variant.
options.explanation: The patient’s family history and preferences still require assessment now. Waiting for reclassification ignores independently relevant risk and a current decision request.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: The specific variant is classified as uncertain.
The gene has recognized disease associations.
The patient is considering an irreversible procedure.
The family history may independently affect risk.
The formal risk assessment is incomplete.
There is no confirmed familial pathogenic variant.
reasoning: Separate gene-level disease association from the classification of the individual variant.
Integrate independent risk, the irreversibility of the decision and patient preferences in a multidisciplinary evaluation.
review.debrief: Keep variant interpretation and whole-person risk assessment connected without collapsing them into the same claim. A cautious interpretation of the variant must still allow timely assessment of independently important risk.
review.conflict: A concerning pedigree and a well-known gene coexist with an uncertain variant that cannot independently justify an irreversible procedure.
review.anticipation: Plan follow-up for reclassification and update the risk discussion when verified evidence changes, while addressing the patient’s current concern.
review.uncertainty: Neither the need for the procedure nor the patient’s overall risk can be determined from this variant report alone.

context: An adult has a confirmed inherited finding relevant to relatives. The patient understands the result but wants time before sharing it with a sibling. A relative asks the nurse to send the report directly and says the sibling’s appointment is tomorrow. The patient is distressed about a family conflict and has not authorized disclosure. The genetics service can offer a family letter and counseling. There is no immediate emergency described.
prompt: How should the nurse handle the request to send this genetic report before the sibling’s appointment?

options.text: Clarify consent privately, offer supported family communication and seek privacy guidance if a disclosure concern remains.
options.explanation: The relative’s deadline does not establish permission to disclose. A private conversation can support the patient’s understanding, concerns and chosen communication while the team follows applicable privacy policy and seeks expert advice for any unresolved duty question.

options.text: Send a limited gene summary to the sibling’s team and discuss full-report permission with the patient afterward.
options.explanation: Even a limited summary may disclose protected information without authorization. The stated benefit and deadline do not by themselves resolve the patient’s consent or the applicable privacy requirements.

options.text: Document the refusal and end discussion of family communication until the patient independently requests it.
options.explanation: Respecting the current decision does not require withdrawing support. Exploring concerns and offering patient-controlled communication can preserve autonomy and potential family benefit without coercion.

options.text: Ask the requesting relative to obtain the sibling’s consent and use that consent to release the patient’s report.
options.explanation: The sibling’s agreement to receive information does not authorize disclosure of this patient’s report. The source patient’s preferences and relevant privacy rules remain central.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: A confirmed result may matter to relatives.
The patient has not authorized disclosure.
A relative is pressuring the team because of a near-term appointment.
The patient is distressed by family conflict.
Counseling and a patient-controlled family letter are available.
reasoning: Distinguish potential family benefit from authorization to disclose this patient’s information.
Support a voluntary communication plan and identify when local privacy or ethics expertise is needed.
review.debrief: Advanced person-centered reasoning holds two legitimate interests in view. Support the potential benefit to relatives through consent-based communication and appropriate expert guidance rather than inferring permission from urgency.
review.conflict: The result could benefit relatives soon, while the informed patient has not authorized sharing and is experiencing family pressure.
review.anticipation: Agree a follow-up opportunity for disclosure support and document preferences so a family deadline does not lead to an unintended release.
review.uncertainty: The scenario does not establish a legal exception to confidentiality; unresolved duties require the relevant institutional and jurisdictional guidance.

context: An older adult has taken the same medicine for years without reported adverse effects. A clinical pharmacogenetic report identifies a potentially relevant metabolism finding. During the past week the patient developed an acute illness with reduced kidney function. A second medicine with a possible interaction was also started. The patient now reports new somnolence and unsteadiness. The nurse is assembling an urgent medication review with the prescriber and pharmacist.
prompt: What should the urgent medication review establish about the new somnolence and unsteadiness?

options.text: Prioritize confirmation of the genetic phenotype and use that result to explain the new symptoms before reviewing interactions.
options.explanation: This gives the genetic finding precedence over current clinical assessment, kidney change and a new interaction. Confirmation may matter, but it should not delay evaluation of current harm or competing causes.

options.text: Use the long period of prior tolerance to focus the review on the new medicine and exclude the established prescription.
options.explanation: Previous tolerance does not clear the established medicine when clearance, illness and interactions have changed. The full regimen may now contribute to harm.

options.text: Use the genetic report to recommend a proportional reduction in the established medicine while arranging kidney follow-up.
options.explanation: A proportional change cannot be inferred from a generic association. The current symptoms and interaction require supervised assessment of the exact drug, report and patient condition rather than an independent genetic-dose calculation.

options.text: Assess current toxicity and competing acute causes, integrating organ function, interactions and the exact genetic finding.
options.explanation: Current symptoms require prompt assessment, while organ function and an interaction can change exposure despite earlier tolerance. The genetic result may contribute, but a coordinated review must evaluate the actual medicines and other acute causes before attributing the problem or selecting a dose change.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: A clinical genetic report may affect interpretation of metabolism.
An acute illness has changed the patient’s condition.
A potentially interacting medicine was added.
New somnolence and unsteadiness suggest current harm.
reasoning: Recognize that earlier tolerance does not account for changed clearance and interacting treatment.
Evaluate multiple causes of current harm and use genetics as one part of the supervised medication decision.
review.debrief: Clinical context changes the meaning of a stable prescription. Integrate genetic evidence with the current patient and regimen, and evaluate harm before choosing a narrow causal explanation.
review.conflict: Long prior tolerance is reassuring, but current symptoms, organ dysfunction and a new interaction suggest a substantially different risk state.
review.anticipation: Monitor the clinical trajectory and reassess after team-directed changes, with escalation for worsening consciousness or other acute deterioration.
review.uncertainty: The actual drug, concentration, genotype interpretation and examination are needed before assigning a cause or specifying a dose change.

context: A patient brings a consumer report showing no detected variant in a cancer-associated gene. Their sibling has a clinical report identifying a pathogenic variant in that gene. The consumer report states that selected variants were tested rather than the full gene. The patient does not know whether the sibling’s exact variant was included. There is also a family history of early-onset cancer. The patient asks to cancel a clinical genetics appointment because both reports mention the same gene.
prompt: How should the team determine whether the consumer result excludes the sibling’s familial variant?

options.text: Treat the sibling’s result as proof that this patient carries the variant and proceed with a carrier-specific care plan.
options.explanation: A relative’s result establishes a familial finding, not this patient’s genotype. Clinical evaluation and appropriate testing are needed before assigning the individual result.

options.text: Repeat the consumer test with a fresh specimen and use concordant negatives to cancel the genetics appointment.
options.explanation: Repeating the same limited test cannot correct absent variant coverage. Two negative reports may reproduce the same blind spot rather than resolve the discrepancy.

options.text: Verify the exact familial variant and consumer coverage, then arrange appropriate clinical evaluation before changing follow-up.
options.explanation: A negative result is informative only for variants the test can assess. Matching the gene name does not show coverage of the familial variant; verified reports can guide targeted clinical testing and interpretation of family risk.

options.text: Accept the negative consumer result as a true negative because both reports evaluated the same named gene.
options.explanation: The same gene name does not establish the same variant coverage. Treating the reports as equivalent may falsely reassure a person whose familial variant was never assessed.

reflection: What new evidence would make you reconsider this decision?

keyCues: The sibling has a clinically identified pathogenic variant.
The consumer report lists no detected variant.
Only selected variants were assessed by the consumer test.
Coverage of the sibling’s exact variant is unknown.
The patient wants to cancel clinical follow-up.
reasoning: Compare what each report actually tested rather than comparing gene names.
Determine whether the negative result addresses the familial variant and choose a clinical confirmation pathway.
review.debrief: Evaluate test coverage before interpreting disagreement. A negative finding can be falsely reassuring when the clinically relevant target was not included in the test.
review.conflict: The negative consumer report appears to contradict a clinically confirmed family finding, but variant coverage has not been established.
review.anticipation: Preserve appropriate follow-up until a verified clinical interpretation addresses the familial variant and the patient’s risk.
review.uncertainty: The patient’s carrier status cannot be inferred from either the sibling’s result or this limited negative report alone.
